# chatgpt response

I think the basic direction is good. It already feels much more like a real App Store purchase screen than a developer-placeholder screen. The visual language also fits NextSeason: simple, calm, and not trying to turn the purchase into an obnoxious sales pitch.

The strongest part is the **purchase choices**. Annual and Lifetime are unmistakably the primary actions, the teal ties them into the rest of the app, and "$10/year vs. $20 lifetime" is extremely easy to comprehend at a glance. I wouldn't make them smaller or less prominent.

A few things strike me visually, though:

- **The top feels a little crowded.** You have the sheet title, Done button, large green headline, explanatory paragraph, and then the buttons, all in fairly quick succession. None is individually wrong, but the headline is competing a little with "NextSeason Plus" for being the title of the screen. I might give the content just a bit more breathing room below the navigation area.
- **The two purchase buttons look almost *too* identical.** That's not necessarily bad, but there isn't much visual hierarchy between the two choices. Since you presumably don't particularly care which one someone buys, that's defensible. I actually prefer this to the common manipulative "BEST VALUE!!!" treatment.
- **The Restore Purchases treatment is excellent.** Clearly available, clearly secondary, and not buried.
- **The legal area dominates more than it needs to.** Not because of its size—the type size is appropriate—but because it forms one big gray block. Once the wording is revised, I'd see whether it can be visually quieter and perhaps a little more compact.
- **The bottom half is extremely empty.** On this phone that's not harmful, and I'd much rather have empty space than stretch everything artificially to fill the screen. But it contributes to a slight impression that all the UI has been piled into the upper half.
- **The horizontal margins are good.** In particular, I like that Cursor didn't make the purchase buttons nearly edge-to-edge. They feel substantial without looking like giant slabs.
- **The rounded buttons work surprisingly well.** They're more pill-like than most of NextSeason's controls, but for two very prominent purchase actions I think that's appropriate. They feel tappable and friendly rather than "commerce-y."

There is one thing I would change fairly strongly: **the Done button is visually too prominent.** It's a huge white capsule with a shadow, and my eye goes to it almost as readily as the purchase buttons. That's the one element that makes the screen feel less Apple-native to me. A normal navigation-bar-style `Done` button—probably just teal text with an adequate hit target—would get out of the way and let the Plus offer be the focus.

I also think this screen **doesn't need artwork, icons, checkmarks, sparkles, crowns, or a giant app icon**. A lot of subscription screens use those because they're trying to manufacture excitement around a long feature list. Here the proposition is extraordinarily simple: *three shows are free; pay to remove the limit.* The restrained presentation suits that.

So visually, I'd call this **a very solid first pass that needs refinement rather than redesign**. My first changes would be the Done button, some spacing/rhythm adjustments at the top, and making the legal material quieter. I would keep the basic structure and the big teal purchase buttons.

# chatgpt response

Yes, I think **“You can change or cancel at any time.”** is better than trying to describe Apple's UI there.

I checked Apple's current documentation because this is exactly the sort of wording where their requirements matter. Apple says subscriptions can be managed through the user's account settings, and on iPhone the current route is **Settings → [your name] → Subscriptions**. Apple also supports managing subscriptions through the App Store and potentially directly from an app using StoreKit. ([Apple Support](https://support.apple.com/en-us/118428?device-type=iphone&utm_source=chatgpt.com))

So I would make that part read:

> The subscription renews automatically unless you cancel at least 24 hours before the end of the current period. **You can change or cancel at any time.**

That's accurate without tying your disclosure to a particular piece of Apple UI that could change.

One other useful thing I found: Apple's current subscription guidance says the signup screen must show the subscription name/duration, what the user gets, the full renewal price, and a way to restore purchases. Your screen already does those things. The Terms and Privacy Policy links need to be available in the app/app metadata, but Apple doesn't appear to require a mini-tutorial here explaining *where* to cancel. ([Apple Developer](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/subscriptions/?cid=developer80&utm_source=chatgpt.com))

So yes — **I'd let Apple handle the mechanics and keep your sentence short.**
